content:
Long-term arthritis pain affects more than joints. It can affect sleep, mood, relationships and confidence. Talking therapies can help you manage these effects, whatever your age.

This guide explains what talking therapies involve, how they can help with pain, and how to get them. It is educational information, not a diagnosis.

How talking therapies can help

They do not mean the pain is "in your head". They help you work on the thoughts, feelings and habits that build up around pain, such as worry, low mood, avoiding activity or overdoing things. NICE recommends CBT or ACT for people with chronic primary pain, and treatment for depression and anxiety alongside other conditions.

Types of therapy

  • Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT): looks at how thoughts, feelings and actions affect each other.
  • Acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT): focuses on living according to your values while making room for pain.
  • Pain management programmes: group courses, often run by hospital pain teams, combining psychology, exercise and pacing.
  • Counselling: talking through difficulties, such as grief or changes in health.

Getting therapy

In England, you can refer yourself to NHS Talking Therapies online or ask your GP. In Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland, ask your GP about local psychological therapies. Ask whether sessions can be by phone, video or at home if travel is hard.

Making it work for you

  • Tell the therapist about your arthritis and any hearing, sight or memory problems.
  • Ask for shorter sessions or breaks if sitting is painful.
  • Practise between sessions, even briefly.

When to get help

  • Call 999 for chest pain, trouble breathing, signs of a stroke, or a fall with a possible serious injury.
  • Get urgent advice the same day (NHS 111 or your GP) for sudden confusion, a sudden drop in mobility, or a hot, swollen joint with fever.
  • See your GP for a steady decline over weeks, unplanned weight loss or repeated falls.

Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself. Ask your GP or pharmacist for a review.

Common questions

Am I too old for therapy?

No. Talking therapies can help at any age.

Will it stop my medicines?

No. It works alongside other treatments.

What if I do not want to talk in a group?

One-to-one, phone and video options are often available.
